title: The Phoenix
lead: A legendary bird of the ancient world, said to come from Arabia, live five hundred years, die and rise again in a new bird at Heliopolis in Egypt. It is in no book of the Bible. Early Christians, among them 1 Clement 25 and Tertullian, used it as a picture of the resurrection, and some found it in the Greek wording of Psalm 92:12, where the word phoinix also means the date palm.

sections.h: Herodotus and the bird of Heliopolis
sections.b: Herodotus tells the story (Histories 2.73, in Rawlinson's translation). He reports that the people of Heliopolis in Egypt call the phoenix a sacred bird that comes once in five hundred years, when its parent dies, and carries the parent from Arabia to the temple of the Sun, wrapped in myrrh. He says he had seen it only in pictures and did not find the story believable. Kirsopp Lake, in his note on 1 Clement 25:2, names Herodotus and Pliny's Natural History 10.2 among the ancient writers who tell it, "with variations."

1 Clement 25 gives the story a form of its own: the bird builds a tomb of frankincense, myrrh and spices and dies in it; a worm born from its flesh grows into the new bird; the new bird carries the bones of the old to Heliopolis and lays them on the altar of the sun; and the priests check their records and find that five hundred years have passed (1 Clement 25:1–5). The phoenix is a legend, but Clement tells it as fact and draws the lesson that the Creator, who shows a rising even through a bird, will raise those who served him (1 Clement 26:1). The 1 Clement section of this page has more.

Greek phoinix means both the legendary bird and the date palm. The Greek Psalm 92:12 (91:13 in the Septuagint) reads dikaios hōs phoinix anthēsei, "the righteous will flourish like a palm." The site's Hebrew-based wording is "The righteous will sprout like the date palm" (Psalm 92:12). Kirsopp Lake notes that Christians took the Greek verse as support for the phoenix story, and Tertullian read it "The righteous shall flourish like the phœnix" (On the Resurrection of the Flesh 13, in Peter Holmes's translation for the Ante-Nicene Fathers), and made the bird a proof of the resurrection of the flesh.
